guide.heading: How to read the weekly schedule
paragraphs: An off-night is a night with 8 or fewer NHL games. With half the league idle, most fantasy lineups have empty spots, so a player whose team plays that night is far more likely to count than one who plays on a packed 13-game night.
Games per team tells you volume; usable games tell you value. A four-game week spread across quiet nights beats a four-game week where every game lands on a night your lineup is already full.
Back-to-backs matter most for goalies: the second night is usually the backup's start. For skaters they are simply two more games, as long as your lineup has room on both nights.
The schedule updates every night from the NHL, including start-time changes, and weeks run Monday to Sunday with the opening days of the season counted as week 1, the same as Yahoo.

guide.heading: Why schedule fit changes the math
paragraphs: Two players on teams that play the same nights compete for the same lineup spot. Two players whose teams alternate nights can both count. Over a season that adds up to a lot of games that actually count.

Schedule fit compares team calendars inside the dates you choose and counts the nights each pairing covers without a clash. It uses your lineup slots, so a league with more active spots tolerates more overlap.
Use it when you're choosing between two similar pickups, stacking a position, or planning streamers for the fantasy playoffs.

guide.heading: How the draft board ranks players
paragraphs: Rankings start from projected points per game under your league's scoring, not a generic points total, so a hits-and-blocks league and a goals-and-assists league produce different boards.

Each player is then valued over a replacement at his position, and adjusted for how many of his team's games are likely to fit your lineup: off-night games and fantasy playoff games count for more than games on packed nights.
You can swap in your own projection files or a consensus of several, and the board rescores them with your league settings.

guide.heading: What a comparison accounts for
paragraphs: Points per game is where a comparison starts. Cracked Ice then scores both players with your league's categories, checks how many of their remaining games your lineup can actually use, and weighs the games that fall in your fantasy playoffs.
Position matters too: a center who is also wing-eligible fills more lineup holes than one who isn't, and a thin position raises the value of the better option.
The verdict explains which of those factors decided it, so you can overrule it when you know something the numbers don't.

/methodology.title: How Cracked Ice Works: Data & Methodology | Cracked Ice
/methodology.description: Where Cracked Ice's NHL data comes from, when it refreshes, how off-nights, usable games and projections are calculated, and what the numbers can't tell you.
/methodology.heading: How Cracked Ice works

sections.heading: Where the data comes from
paragraphs: Schedules, game results, player stats and team stats come from the NHL's public data (api-web.nhle.com and api.nhle.com). Position eligibility comes from Yahoo's public draft data, matched to NHL players by name and team. Nothing on the public pages uses your league's private data.
Your roster, scoring settings and lineup slots are only used for your own views: they stay in your browser, or in your account if you sign in.

sections.heading: When it refreshes
paragraphs: Everything refreshes once a night, around 4 to 5 AM Eastern: the schedule first (including start-time changes), then player and team stats, eligibility and injury designations. The site rebuilds after the refresh, so this week's schedule summary on the Season page is always the current week.
Late scratches, goalie announcements and lineup changes made after the refresh won't show until the next night.

sections.heading: Off-nights, packed nights and weeks
paragraphs: An off-night is a night with 8 or fewer NHL games; a packed night has 13 or more. Fantasy weeks run Monday to Sunday, and the opening days of the season (Tuesday to Sunday) count as week 1, the same as Yahoo.
Default fantasy playoffs for 2026–27 are March 22 to April 10 (weeks 26 to 28). If your league's playoffs are different, set your own weeks and every playoff number follows them.

sections.heading: Usable games, not just games
paragraphs: A game only helps you if the player is in your lineup that night. For each night, Cracked Ice works out the best legal lineup from your roster and slots, and counts a game as usable only when the player makes that lineup. The same calculation drives streaming suggestions, schedule fit and player comparisons.
Goalie starts are estimated from each goalie's share of his team's starts so far this season.

sections.heading: Points per game and projections
paragraphs: Fantasy points per game use your league's own scoring categories: goals, assists, points, plus/minus, penalty minutes, power-play and shorthanded goals, assists and points, game-winning goals, shots, hits, blocks, faceoffs won and lost, and for goalies wins, losses, overtime losses, saves, shots against, goals against, shutouts and starts. Rate categories such as shooting % or save % aren't scored per game.

Early in the season a player's rate leans on last season and shifts to this season as games pile up, weighted as if last season were worth 20 games. Players without a full NHL season behind them are topped up with a typical depth player at their position, so a hot first week can't make a rookie the top-rated player.
Recent form (last 7 and 30 days) uses the same categories, so it can be compared directly with the season rate.

sections.heading: What the numbers can't tell you
paragraphs: Projections are estimates, not guarantees. They don't know about injuries or line changes that haven't been reported, your league's waiver order or trade market, or how your opponents will manage their lineups. When you know something the numbers don't, trust it.

author.name: Matt
author.heading: Who writes this
paragraphs: I'm Matt. I write the guides and build the tools on Cracked Ice. Canucks fan, which tells you everything about my relationship with hope.

Everything here starts from one question I kept asking in my own leagues: not how many games a player has, but how many of them I can actually use. If a number looks off, or you want a second opinion on a lineup call, find me on Reddit.
